questions.q: What join type does df1.merge(df2, on="key") perform when how is not specified?
questions.explain: The default for merge is how="inner": only keys present in both tables are kept.

questions.q: What does indicator=True add to the merge result?
options: A _merge column showing whether each row came from both tables, the left only, or the right only
A column with the index of the original table
questions.explain: The _merge column takes the values both, left_only or right_only. Filtering for left_only gives an anti-join.

questions.q: The customers table accidentally lists customer 101 twice. What happens when you merge orders onto it without validate?
options: Ava's orders are repeated once per duplicate customer row, silently inflating the row count
The duplicate customer is dropped automatically
The merge returns an empty table
questions.explain: Duplicate keys on the lookup side multiply matching rows without any warning. validate="m:1" makes pandas raise a MergeError instead.

questions.q: You stack two DataFrames with pd.concat([a, b]) and the index shows repeated labels such as 0, 1, 0, 1. Which argument gives a clean 0, 1, 2, 3 index?
questions.explain: ignore_index=True discards the original labels and renumbers the result from 0.

questions.q: Two tables you merge on customer_id both contain a non-key column named city. What does pandas do by default?
options: Drops one of the city columns
Appends _x and _y suffixes so both columns are kept
Overwrites the left city with the right city
questions.explain: Overlapping column names get _x and _y suffixes by default. Use suffixes=(...) to choose more meaningful ones.
